tasks.tapescript:
Conversation 1 (Q.9-12)

  • M: And today, I’m talking to Angela Morgan. Angela, what made you decide to fly round the world in a helicopter?
  • W: People often ask me why I decided to do it but I’m surprised they don’t ask ‘Why did you wait so long?’ because I’m 57 now. I’m sorry I didn’t do it years ago, because it was such a wonderful experience. But the main purpose for going was to collect £500,000 for sick children by getting different companies to pay us money for each kilometre that we flew.
  • M: And now everyone calls you the flying grandmother!
  • W: Yes, the thing about growing older is that you don’t feel any different inside so you have to do as much as you can while you can. I’m healthy, and my own children are grown up, so I was free to go.
  • M: And what about preparing for the trip?
  • W: Well, it took five months to plan. I was going to go with my husband but he couldn’t take time off work. Instead, I made the trip with my flying teacher who became a great friend while she was teaching me to fly three years ago. I passed my flying test after two weeks; found it quite easy.
  • M: And what was the trip like?
  • W: It was really exciting flying over so many different countries. The only thing was that we weren’t able to spend much time sightseeing because we only stopped to get water and to camp. We took very little with us but we did have tents and cooking things to use at night. We had to spend two days in Thailand because of an engine problem but that was the longest we spent anywhere. Fortunately nothing else went wrong, so we just kept on going after that.
  • M: What did you enjoy most about the trip?
  • W: The most wonderful thing about flying was seeing the differences in the countryside as we flew across 26 countries in 97 days. We flew over oceans and close to mountains; sometimes it was quite frightening, but we didn’t travel when it was dark. We spent several nights camping in the desert and the sky was just full of stars. I made a video of the trip; you’ll see it in a minute.
  • M: Was there anything that you missed while you were away?
  • W: Well, to my surprise I didn’t miss going to work or going out to restaurants or films. The most difficult thing was sitting still all the time. I normally play tennis and swim several times a week, so I started to feel very unfit. I missed hot water and proper showers sometimes too, but not as much as I thought I would!

Conversation 2 (Q.13-16)

  • M: Britta, you’re English, but you live in Berlin. Have you lived here for a long time?
  • W: Well, I was born in England, but I’ve lived in Germany for the past twenty years. I arrived in Berlin about four years ago. Before that, I lived in Bonn for six years, but I work as a journalist and when the newspaper moved to Berlin, I moved with them.
  • M: Were you pleased to come to Berlin?
  • W: Yes, I was. I was looking forward to being in a big city like Berlin. Bonn was quite a lot smaller, so I love the busy atmosphere and all the cultural entertainments here museums, theatres and so on. The only thing I don’t like is the traffic it’s a bit noisy in the mornings. It wakes me up about 6.30, but most days I have to get up early anyway!
  • M: Where do you live in Berlin?
  • W: I have a flat in the old part of the city. It’s right in the centre and it’s not too expensive. It costs me about £500 a month. My street is becoming very popular. There are lots of new art galleries, and small cafés and friendly restaurants everywhere. Eating out in Berlin is fun, and it’s cheap, so it’s something I do quite often.
  • M: How do you find transport in Berlin?
  • W: Well, the transport system here is very good, so I have a tram and bus ticket but in fact, most of the time I cycle. Travel here is much cheaper than in other countries I know perhaps that’s why people don’t walk very much!
  • M: What do you like to do in Berlin at the weekends?
  • W: Well, I like art, so sometimes I go to one of the galleries. I have a nephew called Philippe. He’s only three but he likes coming with me. He likes the café best, I think. And it’s a change from going to the park that’s something he does very often. He usually comes out with me while his parents go shopping.
  • M: Do you miss your friends and family in England?
  • W: I work colleagues socially but I’ve got some very good friends who live in the same street as me. I enjoy meeting people, and I find Berlin is a very friendly city.
  • M: Thank you for talking to us, Britta.

Conversation 3 (Q.17-20)

  • M: Rachel, tell us how your shows for children started. You studied art at college, didn’t you?
  • W: That’s right. But I gave up my career as an artist when my twin daughters were born. Painting took up too much time when I was looking after them. I thought about teaching art classes part-time, but instead I started making dolls for my daughters. I love acting, so I often invented little plays for the dolls, doing the voices myself.
  • M: And when did you start doing shows for other people?
  • W: When our daughters were five, my husband suggested using the dolls to entertain the children at their birthday party. I wrote a little show and he built a dolls’ theatre. My daughters and their friends loved it. As a result, other parents asked me to come and do the show at their children’s parties. That’s how it all began.
  • M: It must be a lot of work for you?
  • W: Yes. I love making the dolls, but I decided that I needed someone to help me with the shows. Luckily my neighbour, Lena, was keen to perform with me. Her husband records the music to go with the shows. It would be impossible to do everything on my own.
  • M: Have you ever had any problems?
  • W: Only once. I did a show for a group of three-year-olds, and I’d written a story about a lion. Unfortunately, the children were really afraid of the lion and started crying. I was worried the parents might complain but luckily they were all able to laugh about it afterwards.
  • M: And what did you learn from that?
  • W: The experience taught me that I had to find out beforehand just what children enjoy. Like me, Lena has two daughters, so whenever we’ve invented a new story we show it to our four girls first. They always tell us exactly what they think of it. And sometimes I take new dolls to the local primary school to check that children like them.
  • M: And the shows continue to be successful?
  • W: They do. I have a range of different shows for five to nine-year-olds. In fact, the shows have become so successful I could do one every day, but I don’t want to do that. The reason the shows have become popular, I think, is because I love every minute of every show and so other people love them too. I certainly didn’t realise when I organised that birthday party for my daughters all those years ago that it would change my life so much!

tasks.tapescript:
Talks/Lectures 1 (Q.21-25)

Transcript

Welcome to this week’s book programme. We’ve got lots of great new books to tell you about. My life, by Joe Wrigley, will keep all fans of Joe’s stories happy for hours. It explains a lot about where his ideas come from and gives a picture of what was happening in his life when he was working on his most successful books. I must say, though, that some of it is difficult to understand if you haven’t read his other books. Now, for those of you who like a good cry Goodbye to the fields, by Susan Marks tells the sad story of John, a small boy who has to leave the countryside he loves when the family move to London because of his father’s job. John and his mother would prefer to stay where they are. It’s a long time before the family begins to feel comfortable living in the big city. There are plenty of books with helpful advice this week. First, the A-Z of photography would make a great present for anyone just starting out with a camera. It has everything you need to know to take really good photos, and learn about cameras, film, lighting and so on. This is not one for the experienced photographer, though there’s not much advanced information here. Turning to the kitchen Cooking for one, by Adrian White, says on its cover that even people who hate cooking will find it useful. A month ago, I couldn’t even boil an egg but now I’m producing all sorts of dishes, some quite difficult and, yes, they taste quite good, too. I’m actually enjoying cooking now I’m now going to try a new book about cooking Italian food. The last book this week is Holidays in Europe, by Mary Curtis. This is an enjoyable read, which will start your imagination working as you plan for next year’s holiday. It doesn’t matter that the writer doesn’t talk about the famous places everyone visits but describes lots of small places away from the main tourist areas. The maps are too small to be useful but the book is still good value for money. That’s it for this week, then. Next week, there’s a special report on giving books as presents, so if you’ve saved up your money and you’re wondering what to get for a friend or relation for their birthdays, you might get some good ideas … I’ll look forward to talking to you then …

Talks/Lectures 2 (Q.26-30)

Transcript

People always ask me why I only travel the hard way! A lot of television travel programmes are about relaxing holidays on the beach but I’ve only ever made documentaries about really long trips. The last trip I did was a 50,000-mile journey around the Pacific Ocean and it took 12 months. But then my very first trip was a ‘round the world’ journey, and the most difficult one was probably a car journey from the North Pole to the South Pole! As you can imagine, I’ve seen a lot of the world! I’m lucky to be in really excellent health, but life is very short and I’ve done so much travelling that I want a change. Travelling long distances makes you extremely tired, and although it’s still a great pleasure for me I want to do something more relaxing now. I think my next travel series might be made nearer England. There’s some really interesting work going on in Wales where they’ve just found what remains of a 2,000-year-old town. Or I might do something about farms in France or even cycling in Holland. There’s always something to film if you look hard enough! But I hope the programmes I’ve made about the really long trips will encourage other people to get on a plane and have some adventures. Some people seem to be afraid of going to a strange country and perhaps being ill there but maybe they realise now that if I can do these trips, so can they. I’m only a very ordinary person. Obviously, you don’t have to travel on your own as I always have. I must say that until recently I hadn’t ever worried about being so far from home even when the children were very small. But while I was filming in Borneo last year my wife had to have an emergency operation and it really frightened me because I couldn’t get back to England. Everything was fine in the end but I wouldn’t want to be so far away if anything like that happened to my family again. Perhaps if I spend more time at home I can do more writing. I’ve done two books so far. I write about places I’ve seen and my feelings about them. I don’t think I’ll ever write fiction or poetry but I’d be interested in writing newspaper articles. My family says I’m very difficult to live with when I’m writing at home … perhaps that’s why they’ve never complained about me travelling!

Talks/Lectures 3 (Q.31-35)

Transcript

With us today, to tell us about his trip across Africa is the biologist Paul Hart. We started on the east coast and travelled on foot across Africa to Gabon in the west collecting plants and flowers along the way. It wasn’t easy, but my route crossed a region rich in plants and I chose it because it won’t stay that way for long when more roads are built. It was my only chance to get important information about the natural life of the area. I had a team of eleven scientists. We walked from six in the morning but the forest was so thick it took hours to cut our way through and some days we only walked one kilometre before dark. Fortunately, we carried special equipment that was very light and we took as little food as possible. But we were always tired when we put the tents up at night. Sometimes we saw elephants or lions. They were amazing to watch and never attacked us. Every day, I collected plants and added to my notes. There was so much new information to write down. There were, of course, some low points, especially when I got anxious about the team. It was my job to make sure everyone got home safely. Towards the end of the trip, I suddenly discovered one day that the food had nearly all gone. It was strange because we brought enough dried food with us to last the trip food that wouldn’t ever go bad and we’d stopped at villages for fresh food too. But then I found that some of the team had eaten much more than they were supposed to. I was angry with them because it was a silly thing to do. Then we started walking again. There were no maps for the area, but we had a local guide. Then one of the team got sick and we couldn’t go any further. We let him rest, but he got much worse. Thankfully his life was saved by a fisherman who came along the river in a boat and took him to a doctor in the nearest village. Finally, I returned home and I’m back with my family and friends. I really missed them while I was away. But I learnt so much on the trip and I’m really glad I went. I was asked to go on another trip this time to Australia but I said that I couldn’t because I’m busy here in London. And I think I’ve done enough travelling.

passage.title: Working From Home: The Rise of Remote Work
passage.text:
Remote work means doing a job from home, a co-working space, or anywhere other than a traditional office, using the internet and various software tools to stay connected with colleagues. Job titles that once required a physical presence — customer service, software development, marketing — proved, in many cases, adaptable to a remote format once the right tools were in place. Although some people worked remotely before, the practice became far more common after 2020, when many companies were forced to send employees home for health reasons. Once workers and managers discovered that many tasks could be completed just as well outside the office, some companies decided to keep the arrangement permanently rather than return fully to their previous routines.

Supporters of remote work point to several clear benefits for employees. Workers save time and money by skipping the daily commute, and they often report feeling less stressed without the noise and interruptions of a busy office. A number of surveys report that most employees who have tried remote work would prefer never to return to a full-time office schedule. Parents in particular value the flexibility to arrange their work schedule around school pickups or other family responsibilities. Some studies even suggest that remote workers complete tasks faster, since they face fewer unplanned interruptions from colleagues walking past their desk.

However, working from home also creates real challenges. Many employees say they feel isolated without daily face-to-face contact with coworkers, and small misunderstandings can grow larger when communication happens only through text messages or video calls. Video calls, while useful, cannot fully replace the small, informal conversations that once happened naturally in hallways or break rooms. It can also be difficult to separate work time from personal time when the same room serves as both an office and a living space. New employees, in particular, often struggle to learn company culture and unwritten workplace rules without watching how experienced colleagues behave in person.

Because of these mixed effects, many companies have chosen a middle path called hybrid work, where employees come to the office on certain days and work from home on others. Other companies, especially large technology firms, have announced stricter rules requiring staff to return to the office most of the week, arguing that in-person collaboration produces better creative results. Employees who live far from the office often feel these return-to-office rules most strongly, since the change adds hours of commuting back into their week. These differing policies have sometimes caused tension between managers, who often prefer employees nearby, and workers, who have grown used to the flexibility remote work provided.

Whatever policy a company eventually settles on, few experts expect remote work to disappear completely. Even companies that have called employees back to the office usually allow some remote days, suggesting that a fully rigid, five-day office schedule may belong mostly to the past. Surveys conducted among both managers and employees suggest that most now expect some form of remote or hybrid arrangement to remain standard practice indefinitely. The exact balance between office and home work will likely keep changing for years to come, as companies continue testing what actually works best for their teams.

Chi tiết "nhân viên làm việc từ xa nhận mức lương thấp hơn đáng kể so với nhân viên văn phòng" (Remote employees earn significantly lower salaries than office workers) hoàn toàn không được nhắc đến.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R1Q8): Tập trung vào từ quy chiếu "These" ở đoạn 4 để xác định đối tượng được nhắc đến trước đó: các chính sách làm việc khác nhau giữa các công ty (differing work policies).

passage.title: TikTok's Numbers: Growth, Revenue, and the Risk of Misreading Statistics
passage.text:
TikTok's predecessor, a Shanghai-based app called Douyin, launched domestically in China in September 2016, while the international version debuted the following year and merged in 2018 with Musical.ly, a lip-syncing app already popular among younger users in the United States and Europe. That merger, rather than TikTok's original 2016 launch, is what most analysts credit with triggering the platform's rapid global expansion, since it inherited Musical.ly's existing user base rather than building an international audience from nothing. By 2021, the platform had surpassed one billion monthly active users worldwide, a milestone it reportedly reached faster than any social media platform before it.

Average daily usage figures vary considerably depending on which market and which year's data is cited, a distinction that matters more than casual comparisons often suggest. Global surveys conducted in 2022 placed average daily use at approximately 95 minutes per user, notably higher than the roughly 50 minutes reported for a leading rival short-video feature launched by a competing platform that same year. Usage in certain Southeast Asian markets, however, has been reported at closer to 125 minutes daily, a figure sometimes mistakenly cited as the platform's global average rather than as a regional outlier.

Advertising revenue grew from an estimated 4 billion US dollars in 2020 to roughly 18 billion US dollars by 2022, a near fourfold increase within just two years, before growth moderated somewhat as the advertising market matured and competition for the same advertising budgets intensified. Some industry estimates for 2023 place revenue closer to 20 billion US dollars, a figure that represents continued growth but at a considerably slower rate than the near fourfold jump recorded between 2020 and 2022.

The platform's age demographics have shifted noticeably since its early years. In 2019, users under 18 were estimated to make up roughly 40 percent of the platform's user base in several Western markets, a proportion that had declined to closer to 25 percent by 2023 as older age groups joined in increasing numbers. This shift complicates any claim that TikTok remains primarily a platform for teenagers, even though that early reputation, formed during the 2019 period, continues to shape public perception well after the underlying demographic reality changed.

The recommendation algorithm's ability to infer user preferences from viewing behavior alone, without requiring users to follow accounts or specify interests explicitly, is frequently cited as central to the platform's engagement levels. Internal research reportedly shared with regulators suggested the algorithm could produce a reasonably tailored recommendation feed after as few as eight to ten videos watched, a claim that, if accurate, would represent a substantially faster personalization process than the hundreds of interactions typically required by earlier recommendation systems built around follower networks and explicit likes.

Regulatory scrutiny intensified from 2020 onward, beginning with a since-reversed ban attempt in India in mid-2020 and followed by security reviews in several Western countries concerned about data access by a foreign-owned company. A more sustained ban targeting government devices specifically, rather than the general public, took effect in several countries beginning in early 2023, a more limited measure than the outright national bans some commentators mistakenly assumed had already been implemented nationwide by that point.

Given how rapidly both the platform's user numbers and its regulatory environment have shifted within a single decade, projections about where TikTok's global reach or revenue will stand even five years from now remain, industry analysts generally concede, considerably less reliable than the platform's already-documented growth over its first several years might suggest.

passage.title: Exercise Before Sleep: Reassessing an Old Warning
passage.text:
For decades, sleep hygiene guidelines have cautioned against exercising within several hours of bedtime, a recommendation so consistently repeated across public health materials that few people questioned whether the underlying evidence justified quite so blanket a warning. Only once researchers began systematically comparing exercise timing against objectively measured sleep outcomes, rather than relying on general assumptions about arousal and rest, did the picture begin to look considerably more complicated than the original advice suggested.

The physiological reasoning behind the traditional caution is not unfounded: vigorous exercise raises core body temperature, and because falling body temperature is one of the physiological signals the brain uses to initiate sleep, exercising too close to bedtime could plausibly delay the temperature drop needed for sleep onset. Exercise also triggers a temporary surge in adrenaline and, to a lesser extent, cortisol, both of which promote alertness rather than the physiological winding-down that precedes sleep, which is precisely the combination of effects the original guidelines were designed to avoid.

Systematic reviews published over the past decade, however, have found the actual effect on sleep to be considerably smaller and less consistent than the traditional warning implied. Several meta-analyses report that evening exercise, on average, produces no significant delay in sleep onset and may even modestly improve total sleep time, a finding that directly contradicts the blanket caution still printed in many public health brochures. Whether this discrepancy reflects genuine physiological reality or simply methodological differences between older observational studies and newer controlled trials remains a point some sleep researchers continue to debate.

Much of the apparent contradiction dissolves once timing and intensity are considered separately rather than treated as a single undifferentiated variable. Exercise completed within roughly one hour of bedtime, particularly at high intensity, does appear to delay sleep onset modestly in a meaningful share of study participants, whereas moderate-intensity exercise completed two or more hours before bedtime shows little consistent disruption and, in several studies, correlates with improved sleep quality rather than impaired sleep. This distinction, largely absent from older public health guidance, may explain why so many people report personal experiences that contradict the traditional advice without those experiences necessarily disproving the underlying physiological mechanism.

Individual variation complicates the picture further, since habitual exercisers appear to tolerate evening workouts with considerably less sleep disruption than occasional exercisers attempting a similarly vigorous session, a difference some researchers attribute to physiological adaptation built up through regular training rather than any difference in the exercise itself. Chronotype — whether a person's natural tendency runs toward earlier or later sleep and wake times — also appears to modulate how strongly evening exercise affects sleep onset, though the mechanism connecting chronotype to this sensitivity remains only partially understood.

Sleep specialists have responded to this accumulating evidence by shifting away from the blanket avoidance once universally recommended, instead offering more individualized guidance that accounts for exercise intensity, proximity to bedtime, and a person's own exercise habits and observed sleep response. Some clinicians now recommend that patients experiment cautiously with evening exercise timing rather than assuming, on the basis of decades-old general advice, that any evening exertion will necessarily undermine that night's sleep.

None of this evidence suggests the original caution was entirely mistaken so much as insufficiently specific, since a genuine effect on sleep onset does appear to exist for high-intensity exercise performed very close to bedtime, even as the broader prohibition against any evening exercise whatsoever now looks considerably less justified than it once did. Precisely where the practical threshold lies — how close to bedtime, at what intensity, for which individuals — remains a question researchers are still working to answer with the specificity that clinical guidance ultimately requires.

passage.title: Homeschooling: Motivations, Evidence, and Regulatory Variation
passage.text:
Homeschooling — the practice of educating children primarily at home rather than enrolling them in a public or private school — occupies a peculiar legal position across jurisdictions, tolerated with minimal oversight in some regions while subject to standardized testing requirements, curriculum approval, or periodic assessment in others, a regulatory patchwork that itself complicates any attempt to generalize about homeschooling's effects across the population as a whole.

Parental motivations for choosing homeschooling have diversified considerably since the practice's modern resurgence in the 1970s and 1980s, when religious conviction and dissatisfaction with secular curricula dominated survey responses; more recent motivations increasingly cite dissatisfaction with school safety, a desire to accommodate a child's particular learning needs, or simply a preference for greater flexibility in scheduling and curriculum pacing, though disentangling which motivation predominates in any given period remains complicated by how survey questions themselves have changed over the decades.

Claims that homeschooled children achieve academic outcomes superior to their conventionally schooled peers rest, almost entirely, on studies whose samples are not randomly drawn but instead consist of families who volunteered to participate, a self-selection problem that likely inflates apparent achievement gaps, since families willing to complete standardized assessments and share results with researchers are plausibly more academically engaged, on average, than homeschooling families who decline to participate. Whether homeschooled children genuinely outperform their peers once this selection bias is adequately accounted for remains, several methodologists have noted, a question the existing research base is simply not designed to answer with confidence.

A comparable methodological problem complicates the long-running debate over socialization, in which critics have argued that homeschooled children lack sufficient peer interaction while advocates counter that co-ops, sports leagues, and community activities provide socialization opportunities at least comparable to those a conventional school offers. Existing studies measuring homeschooled children's social skills and emotional adjustment report results that vary considerably depending on which measure of socialization researchers select, which population of homeschoolers they sample, and which comparison group of conventionally schooled peers is used, a degree of methodological inconsistency that makes any confident, generalizable conclusion about socialization outcomes considerably harder to reach than either side of the public debate typically acknowledges.

Enrollment figures suggest homeschooling grew modestly but steadily through the two decades preceding 2020, before rising sharply during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, when school closures prompted many families to try homeschooling out of immediate necessity rather than considered preference. Whether this pandemic-era surge represents a durable shift in how families approach education, or merely a temporary spike that will substantially recede once families judge conventional schooling to have fully normalized again, is a question enrollment data collected several years after the pandemic's peak has only begun, tentatively, to address.

Regulatory approaches to homeschooling vary considerably even within single countries, let alone across them: some jurisdictions require only a simple notification of intent to homeschool, others mandate periodic standardized testing or portfolio review, and a smaller number require homeschooling parents to hold specific educational qualifications before they may legally teach their own children. Advocates for lighter regulation argue that testing requirements disproportionately burden families without meaningfully identifying the small minority of cases where a child's education is genuinely inadequate, whereas proponents of stronger oversight counter that the absence of any assessment mechanism risks leaving inadequately educated children entirely undetected until, in the most severe documented cases, serious harm has already occurred.

Considered together, the research literature on homeschooling supports far fewer confident generalizations than either side of the public debate typically claims, constrained as it is by self-selected samples, inconsistent measurement approaches, and a regulatory landscape too varied to support any single, universally applicable conclusion about outcomes. Whether future research employing more rigorous sampling methods will resolve these persistent uncertainties, or whether the practice's sheer diversity of motivation and implementation will continue to resist any single explanatory framework, remains a question current researchers answer with considerably more caution than the confidence found in most popular commentary on the subject.

tasks.suggestion:
Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

  • Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q3, R4Q4): Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét từ khóa) để tìm kiếm các dữ kiện trực tiếp có sẵn trong bài đọc.
    • Với R4Q2, quét từ khóa "academic outcomes" ở đoạn 3 để tìm nguyên nhân: do mẫu nghiên cứu phụ thuộc vào các gia đình tự nguyện tham gia và có mức độ gắn kết học thuật cao hơn (Because study samples rely on self-selected, more academically engaged families).
    • Với R4Q3, quét cụm từ "pandemic-era rise" ở đoạn 5 để xác định điểm chưa chắc chắn: liệu sự gia tăng này đại diện cho sự thay đổi bền vững hay chỉ là sự bùng phát tạm thời (Whether the rise represents a durable shift or a temporary spike).
    • Với R4Q4, định vị lập luận của bên ủng hộ nới lỏng quy định ở đoạn 6: các yêu cầu kiểm tra gây gánh nặng cho gia đình mà không giúp nhận diện hiệu quả các trường hợp giáo dục yếu kém (Testing requirements burden families without meaningfully identifying inadequate education cases).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính (R4Q1): Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu chủ đề của các đoạn: thiên vị tự chọn (selection bias) và các thước đo không đồng nhất hạn chế đưa ra kết luận chắc chắn về kết quả của giáo dục tại nhà (Selection bias and inconsistent measures limit confident conclusions about homeschooling outcomes).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng theo ngữ cảnh (R4Q6, R4Q7): Sử dụng kỹ năng Context Clues (Manh mối ngữ cảnh).
    • Với R4Q6, từ "disentangling" ở đoạn 2 mô tả việc tách bạch/bóc tách các động lực khác nhau. Ngữ cảnh này đồng nghĩa với phân tách, gỡ rối (separating out).
    • Với R4Q7, từ "durable" ở đoạn 5 mô tả một sự thay đổi mang tính bền vững/lâu dài. Ngữ cảnh này đồng nghĩa với lâu dài, bền vững (lasting).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R4Q5): Đối soát các động cơ học tại nhà ở đoạn 2: niềm tin tôn giáo, sự không hài lòng với an toàn trường học, nhu cầu học tập riêng, và sự linh hoạt về thời gian. Chi tiết "đảm bảo điểm thi chuẩn hóa cao hơn các trường truyền thống" (A guarantee of higher standardized test scores than conventional schools) hoàn toàn không được đề cập.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R4Q8): Từ quy chiếu "this" trong cụm "this selection bias" ở đoạn 3 chỉ trực tiếp hiện tượng thiên vị mẫu do phụ thuộc vào các gia đình tự nguyện tham gia (self-selected volunteer families).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R4Q9): Tổng hợp logic toàn bài về các tuyên bố chắc chắn. Những tuyên bố quả quyết thường vượt quá những gì mà nền tảng nghiên cứu bị hạn chế về phương pháp luận hiện tại có thể chứng minh (Such claims often exceed what the current, methodologically limited research supports).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Cấu trúc lập luận (R4Q10): Phân tích cách tác giả xây dựng bài viết. Tác giả trình bày cơ sở nghiên cứu về giáo dục tại nhà đồng thời liên tục làm nổi bật những hạn chế về mặt phương pháp luận của nó (By presenting homeschooling's research base while consistently highlighting its methodological limitations).

Lời khuyên: Hãy ưu tiên làm trước các câu hỏi định vị thông tin trực tiếp như Quy chiếu (R4Q8) và Từ vựng (R4Q6, R4Q7). Tiếp theo, áp dụng kỹ thuật đọc quét để xử lý nhanh các câu Chi tiết (R4Q2, R4Q3, R4Q4) và Loại trừ (R4Q5). Cuối cùng, kết nối mạch logic toàn bài để chốt chính xác các câu đòi hỏi phân tích chuyên sâu gồm Suy luận (R4Q9), Ý chính toàn bài (R4Q1) và Cấu trúc lập luận (R4Q10).

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Homeschooling research has fully resolved the socialization debate conclusively.
Research proves definitively that homeschooled children always outperform peers.
Regulatory variation is the only factor affecting homeschooling research quality.
Selection bias and inconsistent measures limit confident conclusions about homeschooling outcomes.

questions.question: According to the passage, why might claims of homeschooled children's superior academic outcomes be overstated?
options: Because homeschooling motivations have remained identical since the 1970s.
Because study samples rely on self-selected, more academically engaged families.
Because standardized tests are banned for homeschooled children entirely.
Because homeschooled children are proven to perform worse than peers.

questions.question: According to the passage, what remains uncertain about the pandemic-era rise in homeschooling enrollment?
options: Whether enrollment figures were recorded accurately before 2020.
Whether the rise represents a durable shift or a temporary spike.
Whether school closures were caused by rising homeschooling rates.
Whether homeschooling existed at all before the pandemic began.

questions.question: According to the passage, what do advocates for lighter homeschooling regulation argue?
options: Testing requirements burden families without meaningfully identifying inadequate education cases.
Educational qualifications should be mandatory for all homeschooling parents.
Standardized testing always identifies every case of inadequate education successfully.
No jurisdiction currently requires any notification of homeschooling intent.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT presented as a documented motivation for choosing homeschooling?
options: A desire for greater flexibility in scheduling and pacing.
A guarantee of higher standardized test scores than conventional schools.
Dissatisfaction with school safety or a child's particular learning needs.
Religious conviction and dissatisfaction with secular curricula.

questions.question: The word "disentangling" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: financially supporting
completely ignoring
entangling
separating out

questions.question: The word "durable" in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: temporary
financially costly
durability
lasting

questions.question: The word "this" in paragraph 3 ("this selection bias") refers to _______.
options: self-selected volunteer families
achievement gap size
standardized test results
academic engagement levels

questions.question: What can be inferred from the passage about confident claims regarding homeschooling's effects on children?
options: Such claims often exceed what the current, methodologically limited research supports.
Homeschooled children definitely receive better socialization than schooled peers.
Selection bias caused researchers to invent the socialization debate entirely.
Such claims are entirely fabricated and have no basis in any research.

questions.question: How does the author primarily structure the argument in this passage?
options: By arguing that all homeschooling regulation should be abolished immediately.
By concluding decisively that pandemic-era homeschooling growth will fully reverse.
By proving conclusively that homeschooling produces superior educational outcomes.
By presenting homeschooling's research base while consistently highlighting its methodological limitations.

tasks.title:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. You received an email from your friend, Jack, who is planning a trip to Vietnam from April 1st to April 7th.

He is asking for your advice on travel arrangements and sightseeing. Read part of his email below.
tasks.content:
I'm so excited about my upcoming trip to Vietnam in early April!

  • What is the best way to get around the city and between different regions?
  • Which specific places should I visit during my week-long stay?
  • Are there any interesting museums or exhibitions you recommend?
tasks.description: Write an email responding to Jack. You should write at least 120 words. You don't need to include your name or addresses. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfillment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng đề:

  • Dạng đề: Informal Email (Thư thân mật).
  • Yêu cầu: Trả lời 3 ý chính: phương tiện di chuyển, địa điểm tham quan, và các bảo tàng/triển lãm đặc sắc.
  • Bối cảnh: Chuyến đi diễn ra từ 1/4 đến 7/4 (thời tiết khá đẹp ở cả 2 miền).

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục logic (Organization):

  • Greeting: Dear Jack, / Hi Jack,
  • Opening: Cảm ơn và bày tỏ sự hào hứng. Ví dụ: I'm thrilled to hear you're visiting Vietnam this April!
  • Body Paragraph 1: Trả lời về phương tiện. Ví dụ: For getting around, I suggest using ride-hailing apps like Grab for convenience.
  • Body Paragraph 2: Gợi ý địa điểm và bảo tàng. Ví dụ: You definitely shouldn't miss the War Remnants Museum if you're interested in history.
  • Closing: Chúc chuyến đi tốt đẹp. Ví dụ: I'm sure you'll have an amazing time here.
  • Sign-off: Best wishes, / Take care, [Your Name].

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Sử dụng câu điều kiện và cấu trúc gợi ý: "If I were you...", "I highly recommend...", "You might want to check out...".

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • Ride-hailing apps: Ứng dụng đặt xe
  • Must-see attractions: Những điểm tham quan nhất định phải xem
  • Historical artifacts: Các hiện vật lịch sử
  • Cultural heritage: Di sản văn hóa
  • Breathtaking scenery: Phong cảnh ngoạn mục
  • Local cuisine: Ẩm thực địa phương

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • First and foremost: Đầu tiên và quan trọng nhất
  • In addition: Thêm vào đó
  • Regarding: Về việc...
  • Alternatively: Hoặc là (lựa chọn khác)
  • In short: Tóm lại

Cách diễn đạt cảm xúc (Expressing feelings):

  • I'm so glad: Mình rất vui...
  • It's a great choice: Đó là một lựa chọn tuyệt vời.
  • You'll be amazed by: Bạn sẽ ngạc nhiên bởi...

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Quên không nhắc đến mốc thời gian (1/4 - 7/4) khiến lời khuyên thiếu thực tế.
  • Sử dụng quá nhiều từ ngữ trang trọng (formal) không phù hợp với bạn bè.
  • Viết quá ngắn hoặc không chia đoạn rõ ràng.

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 2 phút cuối:

  • Kiểm tra các động từ khuyết thiếu (should/can/could).
  • Đảm bảo tên các địa danh tại Việt Nam được viết hoa đúng.
  • Đếm số từ (mục tiêu 140-160 từ để an toàn).

6. Tư duy làm bài:

  • Hãy chọn một thành phố cụ thể (Hà Nội hoặc TP.HCM) để lời khuyên về bảo tàng và phương tiện trở nên chi tiết và thuyết phục hơn.

tasks.title: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
tasks.content:
Online learning has become an integral part of modern education, especially with the rapid development of technology.

While many students and teachers embrace this new method, others remain concerned about its effectiveness compared to traditional classrooms.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of online learning.
tasks.description: Write an essay to an educated reader to discuss the advantages and disadvantages of online learning. Include reasons and any relevant examples to support your answer. You should write at least 250 words. Your response will be evaluated in terms of Task Fulfilment, Organization, Vocabulary and Grammar.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng bài:

  • Dạng bài: Advantages and Disadvantages Essay.
  • Chủ đề: Học trực tuyến (Online learning/E-learning).
  • Yêu cầu: Phân tích cả mặt lợi và mặt hại, không nhất thiết phải nêu quan điểm cá nhân trừ khi đề bài yêu cầu thêm, nhưng nên có sự đánh giá khách quan.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục (Organization):

  • Introduction: Giới thiệu xu hướng học online và nêu rằng nó có cả ưu điểm lẫn nhược điểm. Ví dụ: While online education offers flexibility, it also presents several challenges for learners.
  • Body 1 (Advantages): Sự linh hoạt, tiết kiệm chi phí, nguồn tài liệu phong phú. Ví dụ: The most significant advantage is the flexibility of time and location.
  • Body 2 (Disadvantages): Thiếu tương tác trực tiếp, vấn đề kỹ thuật, yêu cầu tính tự giác cao. Ví dụ: On the other hand, a major drawback is the lack of face-to-face interaction between teachers and students.
  • Conclusion: Tóm tắt lại các ý chính và đưa ra nhận định chung về tương lai của giáo dục trực tuyến.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Sử dụng các cấu trúc đối lập (In spite of, However) và các từ vựng chuyên ngành giáo dục/công nghệ.

Từ vựng quan trọng:

  • Virtual classroom: Lớp học ảo
  • Self-paced learning: Tự học theo tốc độ cá nhân
  • Geographical barriers: Rào cản địa lý
  • Technical glitches: Lỗi kỹ thuật
  • Digital literacy: Kiến thức về kỹ thuật số
  • Sense of isolation: Cảm giác bị cô lập

Từ nối (Linking words):

  • On the positive side: Về mặt tích cực
  • Conversely: Ngược lại
  • Furthermore: Hơn nữa
  • As a consequence: Kết quả là
  • Despite these drawbacks: Mặc dù có những nhược điểm này
  • To sum up: Tóm lại

Diễn đạt lại ý (Paraphrasing):

  • Online learning: Thay bằng "distance education", "web-based learning" hoặc "e-learning platforms".
  • Traditional classes: Thay bằng "conventional classrooms" hoặc "physical educational settings".
  • Advantages: Thay bằng "merits", "benefits" hoặc "strengths".

Cách diễn đạt ý kiến / so sánh / giải pháp:

  • It is widely argued that: Nhiều người cho rằng...
  • Another point to consider is: Một điểm khác cần xem xét là...
  • The pros outweigh the cons: Lợi ích vượt trội hơn tác hại.

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ liệt kê ưu điểm mà bỏ qua nhược điểm (hoặc ngược lại).
  • Viết đoạn văn quá dài mà không có câu chủ đề rõ ràng.
  • Dùng ví dụ quá cá nhân (không mang tính học thuật).

5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 3–5 phút cuối:

  • Kiểm tra tính nhất quán của quan điểm.
  • Rà soát lỗi mạo từ (a, an, the) và danh từ không đếm được (information, knowledge).
  • Đảm bảo đã đủ số lượng từ quy định (250 từ).

6. Tư duy làm bài:

  • Hãy cố gắng cân bằng độ dài giữa hai đoạn thân bài để bài viết trông chuyên nghiệp và khách quan hơn.

questions: What kind of books do you like to read?
What kind of books do you think children should read?
Why do you think reading is important, especially for children?
Do you get along well with your neighbors?
What do you like most about your neighbors?
Is there anything about your neighbors that you don't really like?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Phần thi này có 2 chủ đề nhỏ: Topic A (Books) và Topic B (Neighbors).
  • Topic A (Books): Ba câu hỏi đầu kiểm tra khả năng nói về sở thích đọc sách, loại sách phù hợp cho trẻ em và tầm quan trọng của việc đọc sách.
  • Topic B (Neighbors): Ba câu hỏi sau kiểm tra khả năng mô tả mối quan hệ với hàng xóm, những điểm thích và không thích ở họ.
  • Tiêu chí đánh giá gồm Fluency, Vocabulary, Grammar và Pronunciation.
  • Thời gian Part 1 là 3 phút, nên dành khoảng 25–35 giây cho mỗi câu hỏi, cân bằng đều giữa hai chủ đề.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc Answer – Reason – Example (ARE) để trả lời đầy đủ và có chiều sâu.
  • Ví dụ Topic A: "I mostly enjoy reading self-help books and novels because they give me new perspectives and help me relax after a long day."
  • Ví dụ Topic B: "I'd say I get along quite well with my neighbors, especially the elderly couple next door who are always friendly and willing to help."
  • Luôn tự hỏi Why?/How? để mở rộng câu trả lời, tránh nói quá ngắn.
  • Khi chuyển từ Topic A sang Topic B, dùng câu chuyển ý tự nhiên như "Besides reading, I'd also like to share a bit about my relationship with my neighbors."

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Duy trì tốc độ nói ổn định, dùng từ đệm để tránh khoảng lặng dài.
  • Dùng hiện tại đơn khi nói về thói quen đọc sách và quan hệ hàng xóm, dùng should khi đưa ra đề xuất về sách cho trẻ em.
  • Nếu bí từ, hãy diễn đạt bằng từ đơn giản hơn thay vì im lặng.
  • Từ vựng cho Topic A: broaden one's knowledge, age-appropriate content, foster a love of reading, an educational story.
  • Từ vựng cho Topic B: a friendly neighborhood, lend a helping hand, respect one's privacy, a noisy household.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • broaden one's knowledge (mở rộng kiến thức)
  • age-appropriate content (nội dung phù hợp với lứa tuổi)
  • foster a love of reading (nuôi dưỡng tình yêu đọc sách)
  • a friendly neighborhood (một khu xóm thân thiện)
  • lend a helping hand (giúp đỡ ai đó)
  • respect one's privacy (tôn trọng sự riêng tư của ai đó)

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • Firstly - trước hết, dùng để mở đầu ý.
  • Besides - bên cạnh đó, dùng để bổ sung ý.
  • For example - ví dụ như, dùng khi minh họa.
  • However - tuy nhiên, dùng khi đối chiếu ý kiến.
  • That's why - đó là lý do vì sao, dùng để nêu kết quả.

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • Personally, I think... Ví dụ: "Personally, I think children should read stories that teach moral lessons in a fun way."
  • In my opinion... Ví dụ: "In my opinion, having good neighbors makes a huge difference in daily life."
  • I would say that... Ví dụ: "I would say that my neighbors are generally considerate, though sometimes their kids can be a bit noisy."

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Trả lời "Yes"/"No" rồi im lặng mà không giải thích thêm - lỗi nghiêm trọng nhất.
  • Ở Topic A, chỉ nêu tên thể loại sách mà không giải thích lý do phù hợp với trẻ em.
  • Ở Topic B, chỉ nói chung chung "good"/"bad" mà không đưa ra ví dụ cụ thể.
  • Phát âm sai trọng âm từ: 'neighbor, edu'cational.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Dùng câu đệm: "That's an interesting question, let me think for a second."
  • Nếu quên từ, hãy mô tả khái niệm bằng từ đơn giản hơn.
  • Với Topic A, nếu bí ý, hãy kể tên một cuốn sách cụ thể và tóm tắt ngắn gọn nội dung.
  • Với Topic B, nếu bí ý, hãy kể về một kỷ niệm cụ thể với hàng xóm.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Coi đây như một cuộc trò chuyện thân mật với giám khảo, không phải bài kiểm tra căng thẳng.
  • Khi chuyển từ Topic A sang Topic B, hãy "reset" tâm lý để bắt đầu câu chuyện mới.
  • Ưu tiên sự tự nhiên và trôi chảy hơn là cố dùng từ vựng quá phức tạp.

tasks.situation:
Your community center is planning an event for children, but you can only choose one activity to organize.

You are considering the following options:

  • Option 1: Organize mini games
  • Option 2: Organize a self-cooking meal with their child
  • Option 3: Organize a music festival night

Choose the best option and explain your reasons.
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Đây là dạng Solution Discussion. Bạn cần chọn một hoạt động phù hợp nhất để tổ chức sự kiện cho trẻ em trong ba lựa chọn: các trò chơi nhỏ, buổi nấu ăn cùng con, hoặc đêm nhạc hội.
  • Ba lựa chọn khác nhau về tính giáo dục, sự gắn kết gia đình và mức độ giải trí.
  • Thời gian là 4 phút; cần phân tích cả ba phương án trước khi đưa ra kết luận.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc I-C-E (Introduction - Comparison/Body - End) để trình bày mạch lạc từng lựa chọn rồi kết luận.
  • Option 1 (Mini games): "Organizing mini games would keep the children entertained and help them develop teamwork skills, but it might not involve the parents very much."
  • Option 2 (Nấu ăn cùng con): "A self-cooking activity with their child would strengthen the bond between parents and children, though it requires more preparation and supervision."
  • Option 3 (Đêm nhạc hội): "A music festival night would create a fun and lively atmosphere for the whole family, but it may be too overwhelming or too late for younger children."
  • Nên neo lập luận vào bối cảnh thực tế của một sự kiện cộng đồng dành cho gia đình có trẻ nhỏ.
  • Dùng từ nối tương phản như "however", "whereas" để chuyển giữa ưu và nhược điểm của từng lựa chọn.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Liên kết các lựa chọn với nhau thay vì nói tách rời, ví dụ: "Unlike mini games, which mainly involve the children, the cooking activity brings parents and children together."
  • Dùng modal verbs (would, could, should) khi giả định và đề xuất giải pháp.
  • Paraphrase "event" bằng "activity" hoặc "gathering" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • strengthen family bonds (thắt chặt tình cảm gia đình)
  • develop teamwork skills (phát triển kỹ năng làm việc nhóm)
  • a lively atmosphere (một không khí sôi động)
  • hands-on experience (trải nghiệm thực hành)
  • require careful supervision (đòi hỏi sự giám sát cẩn thận)
  • age-appropriate activities (hoạt động phù hợp với lứa tuổi)

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • Compared with - so với, dùng khi so sánh hai lựa chọn.
  • Whereas - trong khi đó, dùng để đối lập.
  • Nevertheless - tuy nhiên, dùng để chuyển ý ngược lại.
  • Taking everything into account - xét tất cả các yếu tố, dùng trước kết luận.
  • In terms of - xét về mặt, dùng khi so sánh theo tiêu chí cụ thể.

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • If I had to choose, I would go with... Ví dụ: "If I had to choose, I would go with the cooking activity because it creates a meaningful bonding experience for families."
  • I'm more inclined towards... Ví dụ: "I'm more inclined towards something that involves both parents and children rather than just entertainment."
  • All things considered... Ví dụ: "All things considered, the mini games seem like the most practical choice given the limited budget."

4. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Chỉ khen lựa chọn mình chọn mà không phân tích nhược điểm của nó.
  • Lặp lại từ "fun"/"good" quá nhiều thay vì dùng tính từ học thuật hơn.
  • Không có kết luận rõ ràng ở cuối bài nói.

5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Nếu quên từ vựng liên quan đến một lựa chọn, chuyển hướng sang nói về chi phí tổ chức hoặc độ an toàn cho trẻ.
  • Dùng câu chờ ý: "Let's evaluate this option from a different perspective."
  • Nếu bí ý ở một lựa chọn, hãy bình tĩnh chuyển sang phân tích lựa chọn tiếp theo.

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Đặt mình vào vị trí ban tổ chức - hoạt động nào vừa an toàn, vừa mang lại giá trị lâu dài cho trẻ em và gia đình?
  • Có thể đề xuất kết hợp, ví dụ chơi mini games trước rồi cùng nấu ăn, để thể hiện tư duy linh hoạt.
  • Đưa ra một vài gợi ý cải thiện ngay cả với lựa chọn đã chọn để thể hiện tư duy phản biện.

tasks.topic: Reasons for job loss among young people

mindmap.title: Job Loss Among Youth
ideas: Health issues that are not guaranteed

followUp: What do young people need to do to get a good job?
How can workplace conflicts be avoided or resolved?
Do you think schools prepare students well enough for the job market?
tasks.suggestion:
1. Phân tích đề bài:

  • Chủ đề yêu cầu bạn phát triển bài nói về các nguyên nhân khiến người trẻ mất việc làm, dựa trên ba nhánh chính và một nhánh ý kiến cá nhân.
  • Ba nhánh chính gồm: xung đột nơi làm việc, vấn đề sức khỏe không đảm bảo, và thiếu kỹ năng cần thiết dẫn đến mất việc.
  • Gợi ý cho nhánh thứ 4 (ý kiến cá nhân): có thể phát triển theo hướng ảnh hưởng của sự thay đổi công nghệ hoặc tự động hóa đến cơ hội việc làm của người trẻ.
  • Thời gian là 5 phút: khoảng 3–3.5 phút cho bài nói chính, phần còn lại dành cho câu hỏi follow-up.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):

  • Sử dụng cấu trúc IDEA (Introduction – Detail – Example – Add/wrap up) để trình bày từng nhánh của sơ đồ tư duy.
  • Ví dụ mở bài: "Today, I'd like to talk about the main reasons why young people often lose their jobs."
  • Ví dụ cho nhánh ý kiến cá nhân: "In my opinion, the rapid pace of technological change has also made it harder for young employees to keep up, which can eventually lead to job loss."
  • Nên đưa ví dụ thực tế như mâu thuẫn với đồng nghiệp, nghỉ việc do sức khỏe kém, hoặc thiếu kỹ năng chuyên môn khi mới ra trường.
  • Bám sát sơ đồ tư duy để tránh lặp ý hoặc lạc đề sang chủ đề khác.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):

  • Dùng các cụm từ chuyển ý mượt mà khi chuyển từ nhánh này sang nhánh khác của sơ đồ tư duy.
  • Về thì: dùng hiện tại đơn cho sự thật chung, dùng hiện tại hoàn thành khi nói về xu hướng thị trường lao động đã thay đổi theo thời gian.
  • Paraphrase "job loss" bằng "unemployment" hoặc "losing one's position" để tránh lặp từ.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:

  • workplace conflicts (mâu thuẫn nơi làm việc)
  • a lack of relevant skills (thiếu kỹ năng liên quan)
  • health complications (các vấn đề sức khỏe phức tạp)
  • fall behind in the job market (tụt hậu trong thị trường việc làm)
  • professional development (phát triển chuyên môn)
  • job security (sự đảm bảo việc làm)

Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):

  • To begin with - trước hết, dùng để mở đầu nhánh đầu tiên.
  • Moving on to - chuyển sang, dùng khi chuyển nhánh ý.
  • Furthermore - hơn nữa, dùng để bổ sung ý.
  • In addition to that - thêm vào đó, dùng để mở rộng ý.
  • To sum up - tóm lại, dùng khi kết luận.

Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:

  • I firmly believe that... Ví dụ: "I firmly believe that developing soft skills is just as important as technical knowledge for keeping a job."
  • It seems to me that... Ví dụ: "It seems to me that many young employees underestimate the importance of good communication at work."
  • What strikes me most is... Ví dụ: "What strikes me most is how a single health issue can disrupt an entire career path."

4. Gợi ý trả lời câu hỏi follow-up:

  • "What do young people need to do to get a good job?" - Có thể đề cập đến việc trau dồi kỹ năng chuyên môn, rèn luyện kỹ năng mềm và chủ động tích lũy kinh nghiệm thực tế qua thực tập.
  • "How can workplace conflicts be avoided or resolved?" - Có thể nhấn mạnh vào giao tiếp cởi mở, lắng nghe đồng nghiệp và tìm kiếm sự hỗ trợ từ cấp quản lý khi cần.
  • "Do you think schools prepare students well enough for the job market?" - Có thể so sánh giữa kiến thức lý thuyết được dạy ở trường và những kỹ năng thực tế mà nhà tuyển dụng yêu cầu.

5. Các lỗi thường gặp:

  • Liệt kê nguyên nhân mà không giải thích cụ thể - luôn cần đưa ví dụ minh họa.
  • Quên nhánh ý kiến cá nhân - nên chuẩn bị trước nhánh thứ tư này.
  • Nói quá dài ở phần mở đầu khiến không còn thời gian trả lời câu hỏi follow-up.

6. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:

  • Neo vào trải nghiệm cá nhân hoặc quan sát thực tế khi bí ý, ví dụ câu chuyện của bạn bè hoặc người quen đã từng mất việc.
  • Câu chờ ý học thuật: "That is a complex issue. If we evaluate it from an economic perspective..."
  • Dùng từ đồng nghĩa hoặc mô tả đơn giản nếu quên từ vựng chuyên môn.

7. Tư duy làm bài nói:

  • Suy nghĩ thực tế và liên hệ với thị trường lao động cạnh tranh hiện nay.
  • Sự mạch lạc và logic trong cách triển khai ý là yếu tố quyết định điểm số.
  • Luôn giữ giọng điệu tự nhiên, tránh đọc thuộc lòng như một bài văn mẫu.
